title.en: The Twelve Sacred Krisses of Lombok: One Needle for Every Head
title.zh: 龍目島十二聖克利斯：每人一針

region.zh: 龍目島馬塔蘭（薩薩克之地）

texts.period: Sasak tradition as narrated by A. R. Wallace, The Malay Archipelago (1869), the Lombok chapters

source.work: Alfred Russel Wallace, The Malay Archipelago (1869), vol. I, the Lombok chapters (the twelve sacred krisses)

summary.en: Wallace's great myth-narrative of Sasak Lombok: climbing the sacred mountain, the Rajah falls into a trance and is shown the coming plague by 'the great spirit, with a face like burnished gold.' The escape is institutional: every village must send one needle for every head of its people; twelve krisses are forged from the counted needles in sight of all men; and when sickness appears, the kris cures only if the count was exact — the myth of a census that carries both salvation and the tax-gatherer's power.
summary.zh: 華萊士所述薩薩克龍目之偉大神話：拉賈登聖山入恍惚之境，『面如磨金之偉靈』示以將臨之瘟疫。救贖乃制度性的：每村須按人口繳針一根；以清點之針，於眾目睽睽之下鍛成十二把克利斯；疾病若至，唯針數無誤之村方能得克利斯之效——此乃『戶籍即救恩亦即稅吏之權』的神話。

sensitivity.note: Wallace's narrative reconstruction of Lombok tradition (1869); read as a literary rendering of a ritual myth, flagged for its colonial narrating position.

narrative.en:
Wallace's Lombok chapters open with the fullest English telling of a Sasak ritual myth — the pilgrimage of the Rajah of Lombok and the forging of the twelve sacred krisses.

BEGINNING: THE SUMMONS AND THE PILGRIMAGE. A great spirit bids the Rajah undertake the journey up the mountain; the whole island prepares — cattle killed and meat salted, peppers and sweet potatoes gathered, betel nuts climbed for, sirih-leaf bundled, tobacco pouches and lime boxes filled for the journey. On the eve of the start the chiefs encamp at Mataram under the tall waringin-trees, and with blazing fires fright away 'the ghouls and evil spirits that nightly haunt the gloomy avenues.' In the morning a great procession of princes on black horses with tails sweeping the ground conducts the Rajah toward the mountain.

MIDDLE: THE TRANCE AND THE COMMAND. On the mountain-top the Rajah falls into a trance: the great spirit appears with a face like burnished gold and warns that plague, sickness and fevers are coming upon all the earth — men, horses and cattle — but that the people of Lombok, having obeyed by coming up to the great mountain, may learn the escape. The command is precise and strange: twelve sacred krisses are to be made, and to make them every village and every district must send a bundle of needles — a needle for every head in the village.

END: THE FORGE AND THE VIRTUE. Every village hastens to collect needles exactly, fearing that one needle wanting would ruin the whole village; the head men bring their bundles to Mataram, and the Rajah stores them with his own hands in a camphor-wood chest with silver hinges, each bundle marked with the village and district of its coming. When every village has sent its bundle, the needles are divided into twelve equal parts, and the best steelworker of Mataram brings forge, bellows and hammers to the palace and forges the twelve krisses under the Rajah's eye and in the sight of all men. Wrapped in new silk, they are put away until wanted. And their virtue is conditional: when sickness appears in a village one of the krisses is sent, and 'sometimes the sickness went away, and then the sacred kris was taken back again with great honour' — but when the sickness would not go, 'everybody was convinced that there had been a mistake in the number of needles sent from that village,' and the kris is taken back with heavy hearts, for was not the fault their own? Wallace lets the tale close with its political edge: the needle-count is the census, and the census is the tax — 'the Rajah became very rich, and increased the number of his soldiers, and none of the Rajahs or Sultans among the Malays were so great or powerful as the Rajah of Lombok.'

FUNCTIONS. The myth (1) explains the sacred krisses of Lombok as ritual instruments of plague-control contingent on communal exactness; (2) encodes the theology of counting — the head counted is the head protected and the head taxed; (3) charters the mountain as the seat of the great spirit's speech; and (4) demonstrates, in a single narrative, how ritual, administration and state power braid together in the Sasak kingdom. Wallace's framing matters as much as the tale: he tells the story in quasi-scriptural cadence — 'And when it was quite certain that every village had sent in its bundle...' — and closes it with the census's economic teeth, the tribute compared needle to needle and the under-reporting villages sent back to recount. The needle-count is thus a double charter: a plague-ritual that requires exact communal enumeration, and a fiscal instrument that teaches every village what the ruler knows about its own heads. Read as myth, the krisses give Lombok's Sasak kingdom a theology of precision: the sacred works only when the count is true, and falsehood anywhere in the chain — one needle short, one head unreported — voids the cure for the whole village. Wallace heard the tale as local tradition on the island in the 1850s; its afterlife in print made it the best-known single legend of Lombok in the English-reading world.
narrative.zh: 華萊士龍目章以最完整的英文敘述了薩薩克儀式神話——龍目拉賈的登山與十二聖克利斯的鍛造。開篇：偉靈命拉賈登山；全島備辦——宰牛醃肉、採椒集薯、攀樹取蔞葉、檳榔煙盒皆滿；啟程前夜，酋長宿於馬塔蘭大榕樹下，燃大火以驚走『夜夜出沒於幽暗林道之食屍鬼與惡靈』。晨起大行列：黑鬃曳地之王馬引拉賈登山。中段：山巔拉賈入恍惚，偉靈現——面如磨金——預言瘟疫將臨人畜；然因龍目人遵命登山，得授救法：須鍛聖克利斯十二把，而鍛之之法，乃每村每區按人頭繳針一根。結尾：諸村急急收針、唯恐缺一；頭人親送至馬塔蘭，拉賈親手貯於銀扣樟木箱，各束記村名；針足之日，分為十二份，馬塔蘭最佳鐵匠攜爐、風箱與錘入宮，於眾目下鍛成十二器，裹以新絲待用。其效有條件：村中有疫，遣一器往——『疫或立止，則以大禮迎歸』；若疫不止，『眾人皆信乃針數有誤』，頭人懷沉重之心迎回——豈非己過？華萊士讓故事收束於政治之鋒：點針即點頭，點頭即徵稅——『拉賈因此大富，增兵置馬，馬來諸蘇丹無出其右』。功能：以『社區精確』為條件釋聖克利斯為疫控儀器；立『點數神學』——被點之頭即受護之頭、亦即被稅之頭；以聖山為偉靈發言之座；並於一個敘事中演示儀式、行政與王權在薩薩克王國中如何編織為一。

functions: Explains the sacred krisses of Lombok as plague-controlling instruments contingent on communal exactness
Encodes a theology of counting: the head counted is the head protected and the head taxed
Charters the mountain as the seat of the great spirit's speech
Demonstrates how ritual, census and royal power braid together

variants.name: Wallace's frame narrative
variants.summary: Wallace presents the tale as local Lombok tradition retold in quasi-scriptural style, with his own ironic coda on the tax.

primary_sources.citation: Narrated in Wallace, The Malay Archipelago, London 1869, vol. I, the Lombok chapters (the pilgrimage of the Rajah of Lombok).

secondary_sources.work: Alfred Russel Wallace, The Malay Archipelago
secondary_sources.citation: Wallace 1869, London: Macmillan — vol. I, Lombok: Mataram, the mountain pilgrimage and the krisses.

source_urls.description: Project Gutenberg text of The Malay Archipelago, vol. 1 (1869)

texts.sensitivity_guidance: Living Sasak royal-ritual memory; paraphrase respectfully, note the colonial narrating frame.

passages.text: On the top of the mountain the Rajah fell into a trance, and the great spirit appeared to him with a face like burnished gold, and said: 'Oh Rajah! much plague and sickness and fevers are coming upon all the earth, upon men and upon horses and upon cattle; but as you and your people have obeyed me and have come up to my great mountain, I will teach you how you and all the people of Lombock may escape this plague.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Wallace, The Malay Archipelago (1869), the Lombok kris narrative; not verbatim.

passages.text: The great spirit commanded that twelve sacred krisses should be made, and that to make them every village and every district must send a bundle of needles — a needle for every head in the village. When any grievous disease appeared in any village, one of the sacred krisses should be sent there; and if every house had sent the right number of needles, the disease would immediately cease; but if the number had not been exact, the kris would have no virtue.

All made haste to collect the needles with the greatest accuracy, fearing that if one were wanting the whole village would suffer; the bundles were marked with the names of their villages and kept by the Rajah in a camphor-wood chest, and the best steelworker of Mataram forged the twelve krisses at the palace in the sight of all men. And when any sickness appeared, sometimes it went away and the kris was taken back with great honour — and sometimes it did not, and then everybody was convinced there had been a mistake in the number of needles sent.

title.en: The Pilgrimage of the Rajah: Fires Against the Ghouls of the Avenues
title.zh: 拉賈朝山：以火驅逐林道之鬼

region.en: Mataram and the sacred mountain, Lombok

texts.period: Sasak tradition as narrated by Wallace, The Malay Archipelago (1869)

source.work: Alfred Russel Wallace, The Malay Archipelago (1869), vol. I, the pilgrimage of the Rajah of Lombok

summary.en: The eve-of-departure scene of the Lombok pilgrimage: the chiefs encamp under the waringin-trees of Mataram, and with blazing fires fright away the ghouls and evil spirits that nightly haunt the gloomy avenues — the whole island provisioning the king's ascent of the sacred mountain, where the great spirit waits to speak.
summary.zh: 龍目朝山啟程前夜之景：酋長宿營於馬塔蘭大榕樹下，燃烈火以驚走『夜夜出沒於幽暗林道之食屍鬼與惡靈』——全島為王者登聖山備辦糧秣，偉靈正候於山巔待發言。

sensitivity.note: Pilgrimage scene in Wallace's narrative; part of the kris-myth cycle.

passages.text: On the day before that appointed for starting, all the chiefs, both great and small, came to Mataram, the abode of the king, with their horses and their servants, and the bearers of their sirih boxes, and their sleeping-mats, and their provisions; and they encamped under the tall waringin-trees that border all the roads about Mataram, and with blazing fires frightened away the ghouls and evil spirits that nightly haunt the gloomy avenues.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Wallace, The Malay Archipelago (1869); not verbatim.

passages.text: In the morning a great procession was formed to conduct the Rajah to the mountain: the royal princes mounted their black horses whose tails swept the ground, and all, even the Rajah, were bare-legged to above the knee, everyone attended by servants bearing his sirih and betel boxes — the king ascending to do honour to the great spirit who had bid him undertake the journey.

title.en: The Lost Chief of Wanumbai: The People Taken Across the Sea
title.zh: 萬努拜失去的酋長：被帶越大海的人們

region.zh: 馬魯古群島阿魯萬努拜

texts.period: Aru tradition told to Wallace, The Malay Archipelago (1869)

source.work: Alfred Russel Wallace, The Malay Archipelago (1869), vol. II, the Aru chapters (Wanumbai tradition)

summary.en: Long ago strangers came to Wanumbai; the chief resisted, there was fighting, and the chief and his people were carried away — or, some say, escaped in his boat and was lost at sea. All believe they still live in some foreign country; the evidence is a hundred fathoms of cloth sent back once by fishermen who met them at sea, and children of the lost people, kept shut in a large box by a Bugis trader at Dobbo. The villagers ask the passing naturalist, who must know, where their chief is now.
summary.zh: 久遠之前，異邦人來到萬努拜；酋長抵抗，因而交戰，酋長與其族人被擄走——另一說：他乘舟遁入大海，一去不返。眾人皆信其仍活在某海外之邦；證據為昔年漁夫海上相遇時託帶之百庹布匹，以及在多波被布吉商人閉於大箱中收藏的『失落者之子』。村人央求過路博物學家——你必無所不知——告知其酋長如今何在。

sensitivity.note: Recorded tradition with trauma at its core (raiding and taking of captives); treated as oral-history myth with care.

passages.text: A long time ago, they said, some strangers came to Aru, and came here to Wanumbai, and the chief of the Wanumbai people did not like them, and wanted them to go away, but they would not go, and so it came to fighting, and many Aru men were killed, and some, along with the chief, were taken prisoners and carried away by the strangers.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Wallace, The Malay Archipelago (1869), the Wanumbai tradition; not verbatim.

passages.text: They all believe that the chief and the people that went with him still live in some foreign country; and if they could but find out where, they would send for them to come back again. As proof of it they tell of the Wokan fishermen who met these lost people in the sea and were given a hundred fathoms of cloth to bring to Wanumbai — which the thieving Wokan men kept and denied — and of the Bugis trader at Dobbo who kept the children of the lost people shut up in a large box and would not let them be seen.

They had sought for their people everywhere — on the land and in the sea, in the forest and on the mountains, in the air and in the sky — and could not find them; therefore they must be in the white man's country, and they begged the visitor, in an imploring tone, to tell them if he knew where their chief and their people now were.

title.en: The Strangers Who Raised the Drowned: Wounds Healed by Spitting
title.zh: 起死回生的異邦人：唾而癒傷

region.zh: 馬魯古群島阿魯萬努拜

texts.period: Aru tradition told to Wallace, The Malay Archipelago (1869)

source.work: Alfred Russel Wallace, The Malay Archipelago (1869), vol. II, the Aru chapters (the superhuman strangers)

summary.en: The Aru telling of the strangers who took their people makes them more than men: 'they were wonderfully strong, and each one could kill a great many Aru men; and when they were wounded, however badly, they spit upon the place, and it immediately became well. And they made a great net of rattans, and entangled their prisoners in it, and sunk them in the water; and the next day, when they pulled the net up on shore, they made the drowned men come to life again, and carried them away.'
summary.zh: 阿魯人敘述擄走族人的異邦人非同凡人：『其力大無比，一人可殺阿魯壯士多人；縱受重傷，一唾即癒。彼等結巨藤網，網羅被俘者沉於水中；翌日收網上岸，令溺者復生，攜之而去。』

sensitivity.note: Resurrection cluster parallel; the strangers are remembered through their miracles, as defeated peoples remember conquerors.

passages.text: They said the strangers were wonderfully strong, and each one could kill a great many Aru men; and when they were wounded, however badly, they spit upon the place, and it immediately became well.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Wallace, The Malay Archipelago (1869), the Aru tradition; not verbatim.

passages.text: They made a great net of rattans, and entangled their prisoners in it, and sunk them in the water; and the next day, when they pulled the net up on shore, they made the drowned men come to life again, and carried them away — the drowned-raising that fixes the strangers beyond the boundary of the human.

title.en: The Making of a Demigod: Wallace Among the Alfuros
title.zh: 半神之鑄造：阿爾弗人中的華萊士

region.zh: 馬魯古群島阿魯萬努拜

texts.period: Observed by Wallace himself, The Malay Archipelago (1869)

source.work: Alfred Russel Wallace, The Malay Archipelago (1869), vol. II, the Aru chapters (Wallace on his own myth-making)

summary.en: A myth observed in the making, by its own future subject: the Aru villagers believe the preserved animals in Wallace's boxes will come to life again; a spell of fine weather at his arrival convinces them he can control the seasons; his walking alone in the forest is a wonder, and every confession of ignorance is taken for a blind — 'you know everything; you make the fine weather for your men to shoot.' Wallace predicts that to the next generation he will have been transformed into a magician, a worker of miracles, and of supernatural knowledge.
summary.zh: 一次由『未來神話主角』親眼記錄的神話鑄造：阿魯村民相信華萊士箱中製成的標本將復活；他抵達時恰逢連日好天，眾人遂信其能掌四季；他獨行於森林一事本身即是奇觀；凡他自承無知，皆被視為掩飾——『你必無所不知；是你為射獵的同伴造了好天氣』。華萊士預言：至下一代，他將被改寫為行奇蹟、具超凡智慧之法師或半神。

sensitivity.note: A reflexive record: the mechanics of myth-making documented by the subject himself.

passages.text: I have no doubt that to the next generation, or even before, I myself shall be transformed into a magician or a demigod, a worker of miracles, and a being of supernatural knowledge. They already believe that all the animals I preserve will come to life again; and to their children it will be related that they actually did so. An unusual spell of fine weather setting in just at my arrival has made them believe I can control the seasons.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Wallace, The Malay Archipelago (1869); not verbatim.

passages.text: The simple circumstance of my always walking alone in the forest is a wonder and a mystery to them, as well as my asking about birds and animals I have not yet seen; every confession of ignorance is thought to be a blind. 'You must know,' say they; 'you know everything: you make the fine weather for your men to shoot, and you know all about our birds and our animals as well as we do.' My very writing materials and books are to them weird things.

title.en: The Offering on the Leaf: A Morsel for the Deity of the Spot
title.zh: 葉上之供：獻給此地之神

region.zh: 南蘇拉威西望加錫近郊森林

texts.period: Custom observed by Wallace, The Malay Archipelago (1869)

source.work: Alfred Russel Wallace, The Malay Archipelago (1869), vol. I, the Macassar chapters (forest offering)

summary.en: At the midday rest in the forest Wallace's Macassar boys would put a minute fragment of rice and meat or fish on a leaf, and lay it on a stone or stump as an offering to the deity of the spot — 'for though nominal Mahometans, the Macassar people retain many pagan superstitions, and are but lax in their religious observances.'
summary.zh: 林中午歇時，華萊士的望加錫僕童會取米與肉或魚之一小片，置於葉上，安放在石頭或樹樁上，作為獻給『此地之神』的供品——『望加錫人雖名義上是穆斯林，卻保留許多異教迷信，宗教儀行亦頗鬆懈』。

sensitivity.note: Everyday syncretic practice recorded 1869; paraphrase respectfully.

passages.text: At such times my Macassar boys would put a minute fragment of rice and meat or fish on a leaf, and lay it on a stone or stump as an offering to the deity of the spot; for though nominal Mahometans, the Macassar people retain many pagan superstitions, and are but lax in their religious observances.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Wallace, The Malay Archipelago (1869); not verbatim.

title.en: The Tiger of Modjo-agong: The Hunt Ring and the Teeth as Charms
title.zh: 摩佐阿貢之虎：圍獵之環與護身之齒

region.zh: 東爪哇溫諾薩蘭附近摩佐阿貢

texts.period: Incident and custom observed by Wallace, The Malay Archipelago (1869)

source.work: Alfred Russel Wallace, The Malay Archipelago (1869), vol. I, the Wonosalem chapters (the tiger hunt)

summary.en: A boy riding home at dusk is carried off and devoured by a tiger half a mile from Modjo-agong; the Waidono gathers seven hundred men, and the ring-hunt closes on the animal — 'they surround a large tract of country, and draw gradually together until the animal is enclosed in a compact ring of armed men; when he sees there is no escape he generally makes a spring, and is received on a dozen spears.' The skin is worthless, but the skull is hacked to pieces — 'to divide the teeth, which are worn as charms.'
summary.zh: 一名少年黃昏騎牛車歸家，於距摩佐阿貢村半里處被虎銜入叢林吞食；瓦伊多諾集七百人圍獵——『圍一大片土地，漸漸收攏，直至猛獸被逼入武裝人群之密環；虎見無路可逃，通常縱身一躍，撞上十數支矛尖，瞬間斃命』。皮毫無價值，而顱骨被砍碎——『為分其齒，齒可佩為護符』。

sensitivity.note: Man-eater and protective-charm custom; presented as historical ethnography.

passages.text: A boy had been killed and eaten by a tiger close to Modjo-agong: he was riding on a cart drawn by bullocks, and was coming home about dusk on the main road, when not half a mile from the village a tiger sprang upon him, carried him off into the jungle close by, and devoured him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Wallace, The Malay Archipelago (1869); not verbatim.

passages.text: The Waidono got together about seven hundred men in chase of the animal, which they found and killed: they surround a large tract of country and draw gradually together until the animal is enclosed in a compact ring of armed men; when he sees there is no escape he generally makes a spring, and is received on a dozen spears. The skin of an animal thus killed is worthless, and the skull was hacked to pieces to divide the teeth, which are worn as charms.

title.en: The Turks, a Race of Giants: Rumour-Made Myths in Matabello
title.zh: 土耳其人乃巨人族：瑪塔貝洛的謠言神話

region.zh: 馬魯古群島瑪塔貝洛群島

texts.period: Beliefs recorded by Wallace, The Malay Archipelago (1869)

source.work: Alfred Russel Wallace, The Malay Archipelago (1869), vol. II, the Goram and Matabello chapters (strange ideas)

summary.en: The Matabello and Goram islanders held that the Russians were not only beaten but wholly converted to Islam, and that 'the Turks are the largest and strongest people in the world — in fact a race of giants; that they eat enormous quantities of meat, and are a most ferocious and irresistible nation.' Wallace guesses the source: Arab priests or hadjis returned from Mecca, echoing the ancient prowess of Turkish armies — a case-study of how news becomes myth in the far islands.
summary.zh: 瑪塔貝洛與戈蘭島民相信：俄人不僅敗於土耳其，且已全數皈依伊斯蘭；又謂『土耳其人是世上最高大最強壯之民族——實為巨人族；食肉無算，兇猛不可抵擋』。華萊士推想其源：阿拉伯教長或自麥加歸來之朝聖者，追述土耳其古軍之威——此為遠島之上『新聞如何化為神話』之標本。

sensitivity.note: Recorded belief-lore about distant peoples; kept as an example of rumour-myth formation, with no endorsement of its claims.

passages.text: The people of Matabello amused me much by their strange ideas concerning the Russian war: they believe that the Russians were not only most thoroughly beaten by the Turks, but were absolutely conquered, and all converted to Islamism; and they can hardly be convinced that such is not the case.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Wallace, The Malay Archipelago (1869); not verbatim.

passages.text: Another of their notions is, that the Turks are the largest and strongest people in the world — in fact a race of giants; that they eat enormous quantities of meat, and are a most ferocious and irresistible nation. Whence such strangely incorrect opinions could have arisen it is difficult to understand, unless they are derived from Arab priests, or hadjis returned from Mecca.
